psxsdk started as software for using the Net Yaroze on Linux. When getting started with a Net Yaroze DTL-H3001, the development environment on modern computers, Linux in particular, was badly lacking. After getting a working compiler with mipsel-ecoff-toolchain, the project grew to cover whatever else came out of making Net Yaroze development work on modern machines, and then to writing the programs themselves in Go and running them in an emulator that can check them. The Net Yaroze might not be the ideal PS1 development environment, but the ability to use it should not be lost to time. The goals have not changed: Software that is cross-platform and easy to build Modern languages with features that help the software last Libraries and tools that are well-defined and well-documented Source code for everything, always available

emu is a rewrite in Go of psxe by Allkern (Lisandro Alarcón), written with psxe as a guide and used under its MIT license (see emu/PSXE-LICENSE.txt). It emulates the CPU, GTE, GPU, SPU (with reverb and gaussian interpolation), CD-ROM drive including XA and CD audio, MDEC, DMA, timers, controllers and memory cards. It was written to be driven from tests rather than played: it runs headless and deterministically, counting emulated cycles with no reference to the wall clock, so a run takes the same course however loaded the host is. emu/emutest wraps it for Go tests. A test boots a machine, runs it against budgets, presses buttons, and asserts on what was printed, what is in memory or what is on screen:m := emutest.Boot(t, emutest.BIOS(emutest.BIOSFromEnv(t)), emutest.Disc("check.cue")) m.RunUntilTTY("Execute !", 10*emutest.Second) m.RunFrames(60) m.Hold(1, emu.ButtonSelect, 10) m.RunUntilTTY("End of Main", 5*emutest.Second) A program that runs an illegal instruction or makes a misaligned access fails the test there, with the registers, the instructions leading up to it and the program's output. The tests package uses this to boot every example and compare screenshots against golden images. The emulator follows psxe closely so the two can be compared one instruction at a time: the flake builds psxe with a patch that writes an instruction trace, psxemu --trace writes the same format, and psxtrace diff reports the first record where they disagree. web compiles the emulator to WebAssembly (using Go's SIMD support for pixel conversion) and runs it in a worker behind the page in web/static. The Pages workflow builds every example's disc and publishes the site on each push to main, and publishes a preview for any pull request that changes an example.

Everything is built with Go 1.27 or newer:git clone https://github.com/ChrisRx/psxsdk cd psxsdk go build -o bin/ ./tools/... go test $(go list ./... | grep -v examples) # or: task test That is enough for the disc and executable tools, the emulator and the host-side tests. Building the examples additionally needs the TinyGo fork that carries the playstation-yaroze target. The Nix flake provides it, along with the cross binutils, go-task, mednafen and a patched psxe for comparison:nix develop # or: direnv allow task discs # every example onto .build/NAME/NAME.cue task test:emu # boot each disc in the emulator and compare screenshots task site site:serve # build the browser demo and serve it on localhost:8000 task test:emu boots with the OpenBIOS image in web/static, or whatever PSX_BIOS names. The memory card test drives Sony's shell, which OpenBIOS does not have, and only runs when PSX_SONY_BIOS points at a Sony BIOS. No Sony BIOS is distributed here. The tools a disc build uses are also declared as Go tools, so inside the module they run without installing anything:go tool mkpsxiso -o game.bin --boot MAIN.EXE ./disc

The yaroze package binds the Net Yaroze library for TinyGo. Nothing in it is implemented in Go: each function is a bodyless declaration resolved by the linker against the fixed addresses of the resident library, exactly as a C program's calls are. The bindings are generated from the SDK's libps.h by hdr2go, and every struct's size is asserted against clang's layout at compile time, so a struct that disagrees with the C one by a byte fails to build rather than producing a disc that draws nothing. Names are kept as the header spells them, so Sony's documentation reads across directly.import "go.chrisrx.dev/psx/yaroze" yaroze.ResetGraph(0) yaroze.GsInitGraph(320, 240, 4, 0, 0) yaroze.FntLoad(960, 256) The examples are ports of Sony's Net Yaroze samples and demos, each putting a different part of the machine to work, and the tutorial starts from nothing.

psxsdk is a Go toolchain for the original PlayStation, built around the Net Yaroze. It covers the whole path from source to screen: Write PlayStation programs in Go, compiled with TinyGo against generated bindings for the Net Yaroze library. Build them into bootable discs with tools that convert executables and write CD-XA images, including streamed XA/STR files and CD audio tracks. Run them in a PlayStation emulator written in Go, which drives the test suite headless and runs in a browser as WebAssembly. Try the examples in your browser: sixteen Net Yaroze programs ported to Go, booting from the discs this repo builds, in the emulator this repo contains, with the open source OpenBIOS. Touch controls are included for phones. Start here How it fits together, the path from a Go source file to a running disc. Getting started, to build the tools and the examples. The tutorial, which writes a first program and puts it on a disc. The examples, sixteen ports running in the browser, with their sources. The tools, for converting executables, writing discs and inspecting the result.

dumpsxiso reads a disc image back. With no --output it lists what the image holds, which is the quickest way to see whether a file landed under the name a program will ask for:$ dumpsxiso game.bin volume MYGAME, 789 blocks system PLAYSTATION created 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z extension CD-XA \MAIN.EXE;1 1251328 bytes LBA 23 \MUSIC.XA;1 9344 bytes LBA 72 raw sectors \SYSTEM.CNF;1 53 bytes LBA 634 \DATA <dir> LBA 21 \DATA\SOUND\SAMPLE1.SEQ;1 5000 bytes LBA 636 With --output the tree is extracted to a directory, and what comes out can be handed straight back to mkpsxiso. A .bin of raw sectors and a .iso of 2048-byte blocks are both accepted; which one it is follows from the image itself. Streamed files come out as the 2336-byte sectors they went in as, recognised by their CD-XA attributes rather than their names. Reading a raw image checks every sector's error detection, so a damaged image is reported rather than quietly extracted. A sector of a filesystem is the kind that is meant to be read correctly or not at all, and a file recovered from a failing one is a file the console itself would refuse.

The eco2exe tool takes a Net Yaroze program and creates a working PSX-EXE executable ready to be used in an emulator (if it supports running bare PSX-EXEs), or built into a disc image to be loaded by a real PlayStation (if it can play burned discs). The input may be the ECOFF produced by the SDK's own toolchain or the ELF produced by TinyGo or a current mipsel-none-elf toolchain. It does this by parsing the compiled program, combining it with the Net Yaroze development library (aka libps.exe) and then converting the combined program to the PSX-EXE executable format. The executable is patched with a startup stub that initializes the library before jumping to the program's entry point.$ eco2exe prog.elf MAIN.EXE created "MAIN.EXE": 47fb1ad6d1aee3c8bdf71bdc2ecd144b Note: The Net Yaroze development library itself is relatively small, so it has been embedded in the eco2exe binary, meaning it doesn't need to be provided by the user!

The Net Yaroze library and SDK objects are ECOFF, a format current binutils no longer links. ecoff2asm converts ECOFF objects and archives to GNU as source, along with an ld script of PROVIDE definitions for every absolute symbol, which is how the libps entry points are described. ecoffcmp checks the conversion: it assembles the output and compares its .text against the original word by word, masking only the immediate fields where ECOFF and ELF keep relocation addends in different places.

elf2exe writes a linked program out as a PSX-EXE, for a program that is the whole of the machine rather than a Net Yaroze one. It is the plain conversion: the loadable image and the entry point go into the 2048-byte header and nothing is added. eco2exe exists because a Net Yaroze program is only half a program, and has to be combined with the library the boot disc leaves resident in RAM; a program that brings its own crt0 and drives the hardware itself needs none of that.$ elf2exe prog.elf MAIN.EXE created "MAIN.EXE": load=0x80010000 entry=0x80010000 8192 bytes, d00f145ee4fd44f1 The input may be ELF or ECOFF, since only the loadable segments and the entry point are read. --stack-addr sets the stack pointer the BIOS installs before jumping to the entry point, which matters only for a program whose crt0 does not set its own.

hdr2go generates Go bindings from a C header. It was written to bind the Net Yaroze library for TinyGo, where the alternative was 166 functions and 30 structs transcribed by hand. Transcription is not safe here. Every struct has to match the C layout byte for byte, because the library reads and writes them directly, and a field at the wrong offset does not fail to compile. It draws nothing. So rather than read the header, hdr2go asks the compiler that will build the code, twice:clang -target mipsel-none-elf -march=mips1 -msoft-float -std=gnu89 -fsyntax-only \ -Xclang -ast-dump=json hdr.c # structure and types clang ... -Xclang -fdump-record-layouts-complete hdr.c # offsets and sizes $ hdr2go --layouts layouts.txt --header libps.h --package libps \ --out libps/zz_generated.go < ast.json 30 structs, 2 aliases, 166 functions (named=31 known=33 sizes=35) Padding the C compiler inserted implicitly is written out explicitly, and each struct's size is asserted against clang's number:var _ [unsafe.Sizeof(GsSPRITE{}) - 36]byte var _ [36 - unsafe.Sizeof(GsSPRITE{})]byte An array cannot have negative length, so the pair fails to compile unless the size is exactly right. This is deliberately not a test: a host toolchain will not compile the bodyless function declarations, and a bare-metal target has nowhere to run one, so an assertion inside the generated file is the only check that runs during the build that matters. Names stay as the header spells them, so the library's documentation reads across directly. The one departure is that a C name beginning with a lowercase letter is capitalised, since Go would otherwise put it out of reach of every other package; //export carries the real symbol either way. Anything the type mapping does not recognise is reported rather than guessed at, and the report names what has to be bound by hand:1 declarations with unmapped types, skipped: GsOT_TAG: uses bitfields, bind by hand 8 unprototyped or variadic, bind by hand: FntPrint int () ... An empty parameter list is the common case there. In this vintage of C it means "unspecified", not "none", so generating a zero-argument binding would produce something that compiles and then passes nothing.

mdecenc encodes PNG, JPEG or GIF pictures, in the order given, into a movie of run-length codes the MDEC decodes as they are, laid out as format/mdec describes. Every picture must be the same size, and each is extended to a multiple of 16 pixels each way. -q sets the quantization scale, from 1 to 63, where higher is smaller and blurrier.$ mdecenc -o MOVIE.MDC frame*.png The mdec example plays one, rendered by its own ray tracer in examples/mdec/gen.

mips1fix rewrites MIPS II trap instructions as nops so that an object built by LLVM for mips1 will run on a PlayStation. LLVM emits a teq after every integer division to catch division by zero. That instruction arrived with MIPS II; a MIPS I core takes a reserved instruction exception instead, and the program stops with no indication of why. GCC does not have the problem, branching around a break instead.$ mips1fix prog.o .text+0x1c50: teq (0x00a001f4) -> nop patched 1 trap instruction(s) A trap and a nop are the same width, so nothing moves and no relocation or symbol needs adjusting. Clang suppresses these with -mno-check-zero-division, but that is an LLVM backend option rather than a target feature and so cannot be reached through TinyGo. Either way, integer division by zero becomes undefined rather than trapping. -n reports without writing.

mkpsxiso builds a PlayStation disc image from a directory. A disc is a .bin of raw 2352-byte CD-ROM XA Mode 2 sectors plus a .cue naming its tracks, not a plain .iso, because the format also has to carry CD audio and streamed XA that will not fit in 2048-byte blocks. The common case is an executable plus the data it loads, so the directory is the interface and no layout file is involved:$ mkpsxiso -o game.bin --boot MAIN.EXE --volume-id MYGAME ./disc created "game.bin": 789 blocks (150 of run-out), "game.cue" The tree is placed on the disc as it appears on disk. Names are folded to the restricted uppercase set ISO 9660 allows and given the ;1 version suffix that PlayStation programs use when opening files, so data/sound/sample1.seq becomes \DATA\SOUND\SAMPLE1.SEQ;1. --boot writes a SYSTEM.CNF naming the executable, unless the tree already has one. -v lists what was placed where: \MAIN.EXE;1 1251328 bytes LBA 23 \MUSIC.XA;1 9344 bytes LBA 72 raw sectors \SYSTEM.CNF;1 53 bytes LBA 634 \DATA <dir> LBA 21 \DATA\SOUND\SAMPLE1.SEQ;1 5000 bytes LBA 636 The image ends with two seconds of empty sectors. A drive reads ahead of the sector it was asked for, and the console reads a file by asking for whole sectors, so a file that ends at the end of the track is one the console cannot finish reading: the request runs into the lead-out and fails, which looks like a file that is present and unreadable. Pressed discs carry a run-out for the same reason. --padding sets how many sectors, and 0 leaves none, which is fine for an image only ever read by an emulator:$ mkpsxiso --padding 0 -o game.bin --boot MAIN.EXE ./disc created "game.bin": 639 blocks, "game.cue" $ mednafen game.cue [CDC] In leadout area: 639 --file DISC=HOST places one more host file at a path on the disc, making the directories on the way, and may be repeated. With it an image needs no directory at all. Registered files A program can declare the files it reads itself, with the disc package, instead of a directory being kept in step with it by hand:import "go.chrisrx.dev/psx/disc" var stone = disc.Register("DATA/STONE.TIM", "data/STONE.TIM") Register is called with two constants in a package-level declaration: the path the file is to have on the disc, and the file on the host that goes there. TinyGo evaluates the call when it compiles the program, so each registration becomes a record of constant data in the executable. When --boot names an executable in the tree, mkpsxiso finds the records in it, places each file from the directory --src names, and once the image is laid out writes the file's first sector and its length back into the record before the executable goes onto the disc. File.Read then reads the file from that sector, through CdControl and CdRead, with no search of the directory, and a file that is missing or misnamed on the host fails the build rather than the program.$ mkpsxiso -v -o game.bin --boot MAIN.EXE --file MAIN.EXE=prog.exe --src ./examples/dungeon \MAIN.EXE;1 1251328 bytes LBA 23 \SYSTEM.CNF;1 53 bytes LBA 634 \DATA <dir> LBA 21 \DATA\STONE.TIM;1 33296 bytes LBA 635 \DATA\STONE.TIM;1 registered by \MAIN.EXE;1 from data/STONE.TIM A registered path that the directory already holds is an error rather than a choice between the two, as is one path registered from two different host files. An executable not built onto a disc this way, or run from the serial loader, sees a zero sector and length, which Placed reports, and Read falls back to CdReadFile by name. Sony exported CdRead but not the CdControl that positions the drive for it, so the TinyGo target's link script provides CdControl, CdControlB, CdIntToPos and CdPosToInt at the addresses the library's own CdReadFile calls, and the yaroze package declares them. The volume descriptor fields are flags: --volume-id, --system-id, --publisher, --preparer and --application. --date sets the volume date, and leaving it unset records no date at all, so the same tree always produces the same bytes. --file-times records each file's own modification time instead, which is honest about the tree but makes the image depend on the mtimes in it. Streamed media Files named .xa or .str are streamed media: XA audio and video are produced as whole 2336-byte Mode 2 sectors with their subheaders already in place, saying which form each sector is and which interleaved channel it belongs to. Those are written through untouched rather than packed into logical blocks, and their directory records carry the CD-XA attributes that mark them Form 2. --raw adds patterns to the set and --no-raw empties it. A file taken for a stream that is not a whole number of sectors is an error rather than a file padded into nonsense. Every image is a CD-XA disc: the CD-XA001 signature in the volume descriptor and the 14-byte attribute block on every directory record, which is what a PlayStation disc carries and what says a file holds a stream. --no-xa leaves both out, for comparing against a plain ISO 9660 writer. Audio tracks --audio appends a CD audio track, which a program plays by its number rather than opening as a file. Input is a WAV file or headerless samples, in both cases 44.1kHz 16-bit stereo, which is the only thing a CD holds. The two second pause the standard requires between the data track and the audio that follows it is inserted automatically, and the .cue describes the result:$ mkpsxiso -o game.bin --boot MAIN.EXE --audio track1.wav --audio track2.wav ./disc created "game.bin": 789 blocks (150 of run-out) and 2 audio track(s), 15489 sectors in all, "game.cue" $ cat game.cue FILE "game.bin" BINARY TRACK 01 MODE2/2352 INDEX 01 00:00:00 TRACK 02 AUDIO INDEX 00 00:10:39 INDEX 01 00:12:39 TRACK 03 AUDIO INDEX 01 01:44:00 Plain ISO 9660 --iso writes plain 2048-byte blocks instead. That cannot represent audio tracks or Form 2 sectors, and says so rather than writing an image missing either, but ordinary ISO 9660 tools can read it, which is how the filesystem is checked against an independent implementation:$ mkpsxiso --iso -o test.iso ./disc $ xorriso -indev test.iso -find / Every image carries the 64-byte string that identifies it as a PlayStation disc, written into the system area at sector 4. This is format identification: without it mednafen cannot tell the image from any other CD-XA disc and rejects it outright with "Could not find a system that supports this CD". It is not a protection bypass, and could not be: an unmodified console decides whether to boot from the wobble encoded in a pressed disc's lead-in groove, a physical property no file can reproduce. Booting on real hardware additionally wants Sony's licence data, which holds the logo shown at startup. That cannot be redistributed, so supply your own copy with --license; it replaces the whole system area.

objdump displays information from ECOFF object files. It is similar in functionality to the objdump included in GNU Binutils (although not intended to be exactly the same). This was built while reverse engineering the Net Yaroze development static library, as the first step towards converting it from the aging ECOFF format to ELF (see ecoff2asm):$ objdump puts.o MIPSEL-BE ECOFF executable - start=0x00000000 size=96 sections=2 Sections: 0 .text len=80 offset=156 0x00000000 0x00000000 1 .rdata len=16 offset=236 0x00000050 0x00000050 Symbols: [ 0] e 0000000000000000 st 0 sc 0 index=FFFFF gcc2_compiled. [ 1] e 0000000000000000 st 0 sc 0 index=FFFFF __gnu_compiled_c [ 2] e 0000000000000000 st 0 sc 0 index=FFFFF $LC0 [ 3] e 0000000000000000 st 6 sc 1 index=0000 puts [ 4] e 0000000000000000 st 0 sc 0 index=FFFFF $L13 [ 5] e 0000000000000000 st 0 sc 0 index=FFFFF $L11 [ 6] e 0000000000000000 st 1 sc 6 index=FFFFF putchar [ 7] l 0000000000000000 st b sc 1 index=0004 puts.c [ 8] l 0000000000000000 st 6 sc 1 index=0002 puts [ 9] l 000000000000004C st 8 sc 1 index=0001 puts [ 10] l 0000000000000000 st 8 sc 1 index=0000 puts.c It uses mewmew's mips library to decode and disassemble the provided file. Adding the -d/-disassemble flag will add the disassembly to the output:... puts: addiu $sp, $sp, 0xFFE8 sw $s0, 0x10($sp) addu $s0, $a0, $zero bne $s0, $zero, 24 sw $ra, 0x14($sp) lui $s0, 0x0 j 0x28 addiu $s0, $s0, 0x50 jal 0x0 sra $a0, $a0, 24 lbu $a0, 0($s0) nop sll $a0, $a0, 24 bne $a0, $zero, -24 addiu $s0, $s0, 0x1 lw $ra, 0x14($sp) lw $s0, 0x10($sp) jr $ra addiu $sp, $sp, 0x18 nop cfc3 $s5, $cp3_9 syscall 0xF9 nop nop

psxemu boots a BIOS in the emulator headless, printing what it writes to the TTY, with a disc in the drive or a PSX-EXE loaded at the shell:$ psxemu --bios openbios.bin --disc .build/check/check.cue --png screen.png --trace, --skip and --count write an instruction trace in the format the patched psxe writes with PSXE_TRACE. --vram dumps VRAM at the end, --png saves what the display shows, --card attaches a memory card image to slot 1, and --cpuprofile profiles the run for go tool pprof.

psxplay runs the emulator in a window, with the keyboard or a gamepad as the pad in port 1 and the SPU's sound on the speakers. It is the desktop counterpart of the player on this site, which runs the same emulator in a browser:$ psxplay .build/check/check.cue OpenBIOS is built in, so no BIOS image is needed; --bios boots another, such as Sony's. --exe loads a PSX-EXE when the BIOS reaches its shell instead of booting a disc, as psxemu --exe does, --card attaches a memory card image to slot 1 and writes it back on exit, --scale sets the window's initial size as a multiple of 320x240, and --mute leaves the sound off. What the BIOS prints to the TTY goes to standard output. The keyboard is laid out as the player has it:KeysPadArrowsD-padZ, X, A, SCross, circle, square, triangleQ, WL1, R11, 2L2, R2Enter, BackspaceStart, Select A gamepad with a standard layout works as itself, with the left stick doubling as the d-pad. F11 toggles full screen and Escape leaves it. In the repository, task play NAME=check builds an example's disc and runs it, with flags after -- passed on: task play NAME=check -- --mute. The window is drawn with Ebitengine, which loads X11, OpenGL and ALSA at run time rather than linking against them, so building needs nothing beyond Go. On Linux the libraries must be on the loader's path to run it; the Nix development shell puts them there.

psxtrace reads the traces psxemu and psxe write. dump prints one as text, diff reports the first record two traces disagree on, and vram compares two VRAM dumps or converts one to an image:PSXE_TRACE=psxe.trace PSXE_TRACE_COUNT=1000000 psxe -a -b bios.bin psxemu --bios bios.bin --trace emu.trace --count 1000000 psxtrace diff psxe.trace emu.trace

The linux version of siocons, found on the psxdev.net forums (and floating around other places), did not initially work when loading a Net Yaroze executable. Even after figuring out a way to make it work, it didn't work for all baud rates, didn't work consistently, and had several huge bugs in how it loaded binaries (it loaded the sections incorrectly in a way that still worked), so sioload was written as a replacement. sioload isn't a full-feature siocons replacement, but a serial executable loader in Go. Unless specified it finds the first available serial port and defaults to a baud rate of 115200:$ sioload --exec main-ecoff It has been reliable at every baud rate tested, using a Net Yaroze DTL-H3050 serial cable through a TRENDnet USB to Serial converter.

The second program draws a cube and turns it with the directional buttons. The cube is a model, and its texture is a picture, and both are files on the disc that the program reads at startup, which is how a program gets anything bigger than its own code into memory. It starts from the module setting up made; a new directory with the same go.mod does as well. The files A model for the PlayStation is a TMD, the format Sony's tools wrote: a list of vertices and normals, and a list of polygons that index them, each with its color or its texture coordinates. A texture is a TIM, a picture in one of the GPU's formats with the place in video memory it is to be loaded to, and its palette if it has one. Save these two beside the program, in a data directory: CUBE.TMD, a cube 128 units along each edge: eight vertices, six normals, and six textured polygons, one for each face. CUBE.TIM, a 64 by 64 texture in 16 colors, with its palette. The texture comes from Sony's own Net Yaroze tutorials, by way of the flying example, which tiles the plane it flies over with it. The cube is written by a short script, which is the whole of the TMD format for a model this simple, and the program, its files and the script are in the repository at docs/tutorial/cube. The program//go:build yaroze // Cube: a textured cube from the disc, turned with the directional buttons. package main import ( "unsafe" "go.chrisrx.dev/psx/disc" "go.chrisrx.dev/psx/yaroze" ) const ( screenW, screenH = 320, 240 // The ordering table holds 1<<otLength depths; one object needs few. otLength = 4 packetMax = 4096 // How far a held button turns the cube each frame, where 4096 is a // whole turn. step = 24 ) // The files on the disc, and the memory they are read into. The drive // delivers whole 2048-byte sectors, so each buffer is a whole number of them, // enough for its file. var ( model = disc.Register("DATA/CUBE.TMD", "data/CUBE.TMD") texture = disc.Register("DATA/CUBE.TIM", "data/CUBE.TIM") modelData [2048]uint32 textureData [4096]uint32 ) var ( ot [2]yaroze.GsOT otTags [2][1 << otLength]yaroze.GsOT_TAG packetArea [2][packetMax / 4]uint32 view yaroze.GsRVIEW2 light yaroze.GsF_LIGHT cube yaroze.GsDOBJ2 coord yaroze.GsCOORDINATE2 image yaroze.GsIMAGE // rotation is which way the cube faces, built up turn by turn; turned // and ls are the frame's working matrices. rotation, turned, ls yaroze.MATRIX padBuf0, padBuf1 *uint8 pathBuf [64]byte textBuf [64]byte ) // The directional buttons, as bits of what padRead returns. const ( padUp = 1 << 12 padRight = 1 << 13 padDown = 1 << 14 padLeft = 1 << 15 ) func main() { yaroze.SetVideoMode(yaroze.MODE_NTSC) yaroze.GsInitGraph(screenW, screenH, yaroze.GsNONINTER|yaroze.GsOFSGPU, 1, 0) yaroze.GsDefDispBuff(0, 0, 0, screenH) yaroze.GsInit3D() for i := range ot { ot[i].Length = otLength ot[i].Org = &otTags[i][0] } yaroze.FntLoad(960, 256) // With GsOFSGPU the origin is the middle of the screen, for 3D's sake, // so the text window is placed from there. yaroze.FntOpen(-screenW/2+16, -screenH/2+16, 256, 64, 0, 512) yaroze.GetPadBuf(&padBuf0, &padBuf1) if !load(&model, &modelData[0]) || !load(&texture, &textureData[0]) { yaroze.FntPrint(yaroze.CString(textBuf[:], "could not read the disc")) for { yaroze.FntFlush(-1) yaroze.VSync(0) } } // The texture goes into video memory, at the place the file names and // the model's polygons point to, with its palette. yaroze.GsGetTimInfo(&textureData[1], &image) rect := yaroze.RECT{X: image.Px, Y: image.Py, W: int16(image.Pw), H: int16(image.Ph)} yaroze.LoadImage(&rect, image.Pixel) if image.Pmode&8 != 0 { rect = yaroze.RECT{X: image.Cx, Y: image.Cy, W: int16(image.Cw), H: int16(image.Ch)} yaroze.LoadImage(&rect, image.Clut) } yaroze.DrawSync(0) // The model's offsets become addresses now that it has one, and the // object is linked to the first model in the file, in its own // coordinate system. yaroze.GsMapModelingData(&modelData[1]) yaroze.GsLinkObject4(uint32(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&modelData[3]))), &cube, 0) yaroze.GsInitCoordinate2(nil, &coord) cube.Coord2 = &coord // The camera: back from the origin and a little above it, looking at it. view = yaroze.GsRVIEW2{Vpx: 0, Vpy: -120, Vpz: -320} yaroze.GsSetProjection(240) yaroze.GsSetRefView2(&view) // One light from over the camera's shoulder, and some ambient light, // so that the faces turned away from it are not black. light = yaroze.GsF_LIGHT{Vx: 1, Vy: 1, Vz: 1, R: 0xc0, G: 0xc0, B: 0xc0} yaroze.GsSetFlatLight(0, &light) yaroze.GsSetAmbient(yaroze.ONE/4, yaroze.ONE/4, yaroze.ONE/4) yaroze.GsSetLightMode(0) // Facing straight ahead, with a little of the top and a side showing. rotation = yaroze.MATRIX{M: [3][3]int16{{yaroze.ONE, 0, 0}, {0, yaroze.ONE, 0}, {0, 0, yaroze.ONE}}} turn(&yaroze.SVECTOR{Vx: -step * 12, Vy: step * 12}) hint := yaroze.CString(textBuf[:], "the directions turn the cube") for { pad := padRead() if pad&padUp != 0 { turn(&yaroze.SVECTOR{Vx: -step}) } if pad&padDown != 0 { turn(&yaroze.SVECTOR{Vx: step}) } if pad&padLeft != 0 { turn(&yaroze.SVECTOR{Vy: -step}) } if pad&padRight != 0 { turn(&yaroze.SVECTOR{Vy: step}) } coord.Coord = rotation coord.Flg = 0 active := yaroze.GsGetActiveBuff() yaroze.GsSetWorkBase(yaroze.Packets(&packetArea[active][0])) yaroze.GsClearOt(0, 0, &ot[active]) yaroze.GsGetLs(&coord, &ls) yaroze.GsSetLightMatrix(&ls) yaroze.GsSetLsMatrix(&ls) yaroze.GsSortObject4(&cube, &ot[active], 14-otLength, scratch) yaroze.DrawSync(0) yaroze.VSync(0) yaroze.GsSwapDispBuff() yaroze.GsSortClear(60, 120, 120, &ot[active]) yaroze.GsDrawOt(&ot[active]) yaroze.FntPrint(hint) yaroze.FntFlush(-1) } } // turn rotates the cube by the angles given about the world's axes, which // are the screen's: the new turn is applied after everything so far, so up // always tips the top towards the camera and left always turns the left // side away, however the cube already sits. func turn(by *yaroze.SVECTOR) { var m yaroze.MATRIX yaroze.RotMatrix(by, &m) yaroze.MulMatrix0(&m, &rotation, &turned) rotation = turned } // scratch is the CPU's scratchpad, 1KB of fast memory that GsSortObject4 // uses as its work space. var scratch = (*uint32)(unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(0x1f800000))) // load reads a file off the disc into memory and waits for it, giving up // after a few seconds so that a missing disc shows a message rather than // hanging. func load(f *disc.File, into *uint32) bool { if !f.Read(into, pathBuf[:]) { return false } for range 300 { if yaroze.CdReadSync(1, nil) <= 0 { return true } yaroze.VSync(0) } return false } // padRead returns the buttons held on the first controller, one bit each, // from the buffers the library refreshes every frame. func padRead() uint32 { if padBuf0 == nil { return 0 } at := func(n uintptr) uint32 { return uint32(*(*uint8)(unsafe.Add(unsafe.Pointer(padBuf0), n))) } return ^(at(3) | at(2)<<8) & 0xffff } Getting the files onto the disc Two lines near the top do more than they look like they do:model = disc.Register("DATA/CUBE.TMD", "data/CUBE.TMD") texture = disc.Register("DATA/CUBE.TIM", "data/CUBE.TIM") Each names a path on the disc and the file on the host that goes there. TinyGo works the call out when it compiles the program, so each registration ends up as a small record of constant data in the executable. When mkpsxiso builds the disc it finds the records in the executable it is told to boot, places each file at its path, and once it knows where on the disc each one landed writes the file's first sector and its length back into the record. The program is then built with the knowledge of where its files are, and Read reads a file from that sector directly, without searching the disc's directory for it by name. A file that is missing or misnamed fails the build rather than the program. load wraps Read with the wait every disc read needs. The drive works in the background: Read starts it and returns, and CdReadSync reports whether it has finished, so the program polls it once a frame. Giving up after a few seconds turns a missing disc into a message instead of a hang. The two buffers the files are read into are whole numbers of 2048-byte sectors, because that is what the drive delivers, whatever the file's length. Drawing in three dimensions The library draws models through objects. A GsDOBJ2 ties a model in a TMD to a coordinate system, a GsCOORDINATE2, which holds a matrix saying where the object is and which way it faces. The program links its one object to the one model in the file, after GsMapModelingData has turned the file's offsets into addresses, since the file could have been loaded anywhere. The cube's orientation is a matrix the program keeps, rotation, and turn changes it: RotMatrix makes a matrix for a small turn, with 4096 standing for a whole turn as it does everywhere in the library, and MulMatrix0 multiplies it onto the front of what is there. Multiplying on the front is what makes the controls behave: the new turn is applied after every turn so far, so it is always about the screen's axes, and up always tips the top towards the camera however the cube already sits. Multiplying on the back instead would turn the cube about its own axes, which feels right until it has been tipped over. Each frame the matrix is copied into the coordinate system and Flg set to zero, which tells the library the coordinates changed, so that it works out the object's screen matrix again. GsGetLs fetches that, GsSetLsMatrix hands it to the GTE, the geometry coprocessor that does the arithmetic in fixed point with twelve fractional bits, and GsSortObject4 turns the model into drawing commands and sorts them into the ordering table by depth. Only the faces turned towards the camera are drawn. The GPU decides that by which way round a polygon's corners come out on the screen, so a TMD's polygons have to be written with their corners in a consistent order as seen from outside, which the script that makes the cube is careful about. The camera is a GsRVIEW2: a viewpoint, a point it looks at, and a twist about that line. Here it sits back from the origin and a little above it, looking at the origin, and GsSetProjection sets how strong the perspective is, as the distance from the eye to the screen in the same units. With GsOFSGPU the screen's origin is its middle, which three dimensions want, so the text window's position is counted from there. The light is the simplest the library offers, one flat light shining along a direction, with some ambient light so that the faces turned away from it are not black. Each face has a normal, so each shades by its angle to the light as the cube turns, which is what makes it read as a solid. Trying it in the browser This is the program, built onto a disc as the page describes and booted in the emulator that runs the examples. The arrow keys turn it, or the controller, or the touch pad on a phone. Building and running it The same steps as before, with the two files joining the disc through --src, the directory their registered paths are relative to:tinygo build -target=playstation-yaroze -o prog.elf . go tool mips1fix prog.elf go tool eco2exe prog.elf MAIN.EXE go tool mkpsxiso -v -o cube.bin --boot MAIN.EXE --file MAIN.EXE=MAIN.EXE --src . go tool psxemu --bios openbios.bin --disc cube.cue --png cube.png -v lists what was placed where, with the two registered files among it, and a run in mednafen or the console shows the cube, which the directions turn.

The tutorial writes a PlayStation program in Go from nothing, outside this repository, the way a program of your own would be written. It assumes Go and nothing about the PlayStation. Where the machine's way of doing things differs from what a modern one would do, the page says why, because most of what looks strange about writing for it stops being strange once the reason is known. Setting up: a module of your own with the toolchain as a dependency, the smallest program that puts something on the screen, and the steps that turn it into a disc. A cube from the disc: a textured cube, loaded as a model and a texture off the CD, drawn in 3D and turned with the directional buttons.

A program for the PlayStation is an ordinary Go module. It depends on go.chrisrx.dev/psx for the library bindings, and on the module's tools for turning what the compiler produces into a disc. This page sets one up and gets a line of text on the screen. What you need Go, 1.27 or newer. TinyGo with the playstation-yaroze target, which compiles Go for the console's MIPS processor and links against the Net Yaroze library. tinygo targets | grep playstation shows whether yours has it. An emulator to run the result in. The toolchain has one, psxemu, which runs headless and saves a picture of the screen; mednafen or any other that takes a cue sheet works for playing. A BIOS image. The console's own is Sony's and cannot be distributed, but the open source OpenBIOS boots everything here. The copy the player on this site uses is at openbios.bin. The module Make a directory and a module in it, add the toolchain, and add the tools a build uses as tool dependencies, which go tool then runs without installing anything:mkdir hello && cd hello go mod init example.com/hello go get go.chrisrx.dev/psx go get -tool go.chrisrx.dev/psx/tools/mips1fix go.chrisrx.dev/psx/tools/eco2exe \ go.chrisrx.dev/psx/tools/mkpsxiso go.chrisrx.dev/psx/tools/psxemu curl -LO https://chrisrx.github.io/psxsdk/play/openbios.bin The program One file, main.go://go:build yaroze // Hello: a line of text on the screen. package main import "go.chrisrx.dev/psx/yaroze" const ( screenW, screenH = 320, 240 // The ordering table's size, as a power of two: one entry is enough // for a frame that only clears the screen. otLength = 1 packetMax = 64 ) var ( ot [2]yaroze.GsOT otTags [2][1 << otLength]yaroze.GsOT_TAG packetArea [2][packetMax / 4]uint32 textBuf [32]byte ) func main() { yaroze.SetVideoMode(yaroze.MODE_NTSC) yaroze.GsInitGraph(screenW, screenH, 4, 0, 0) yaroze.GsDefDispBuff(0, 0, 0, screenH) for i := range ot { ot[i].Length = otLength ot[i].Org = &otTags[i][0] } yaroze.FntLoad(960, 256) yaroze.FntOpen(16, 16, 256, 200, 0, 512) hello := yaroze.CString(textBuf[:], "hello from go") for { active := yaroze.GsGetActiveBuff() yaroze.GsSetWorkBase(yaroze.Packets(&packetArea[active][0])) yaroze.GsClearOt(0, 0, &ot[active]) yaroze.DrawSync(0) yaroze.VSync(0) yaroze.GsSwapDispBuff() yaroze.GsSortClear(60, 120, 120, &ot[active]) yaroze.GsDrawOt(&ot[active]) yaroze.FntPrint(hello) yaroze.FntFlush(-1) } } It already has the shape every program has: set up the display, then draw a frame, wait for the screen, and swap, for ever. Three things about it are not how a program for a modern machine would read. Everything is a package-level variable. The machine has two megabytes of RAM, no memory protection and, in this runtime, no garbage collector running, so memory a frame allocates is memory the program never gets back. Declaring the buffers once, as globals, is how the Net Yaroze programs this toolchain descends from did it too, and nothing in the tutorial allocates after startup. The frame is a list before it is a picture. The GPU does not draw what it is told as it is told. A program sorts drawing commands into an ordering table, an array of linked lists indexed by depth, and then hands the table to the GPU, which walks it while the program goes on to the next frame. GsClearOt empties the table, GsSortClear sorts a command that clears the screen to a color into it, and GsDrawOt starts the GPU on it. There are two tables, and two packet areas for the commands themselves, because the GPU is still drawing one frame while the program builds the next. The packet areas are declared as words rather than bytes, and handed over through Packets, because the library stores words into them and the compiler aligns an array of bytes only to a byte. The text goes through the library's font. FntLoad puts the library's 8x8 font into video memory at a corner the display never shows, FntOpen opens a window of text at a position on the screen, and FntPrint writes into it. In C FntPrint is printf-like; here it takes a finished string, which CString copies into a buffer the program owns, with the NUL terminator the library expects. The build constraint on the first line keeps the file out of ordinary Go builds, which cannot compile it: the yaroze package is only there for TinyGo's PlayStation target. go vet ./... and editors then leave it alone. Building it Three steps turn the source into an executable the console boots:tinygo build -target=playstation-yaroze -o prog.elf . go tool mips1fix prog.elf go tool eco2exe prog.elf MAIN.EXE TinyGo compiles and links the program against the Net Yaroze library's addresses. mips1fix replaces the few instructions LLVM emits that the console's R3000A does not have. eco2exe combines the program with the library itself, which a Net Yaroze had resident in RAM and an ordinary console does not, and writes the result as the PSX-EXE the BIOS knows how to load. One more step puts it on a disc:go tool mkpsxiso -o hello.bin --boot MAIN.EXE --file MAIN.EXE=MAIN.EXE --boot writes the SYSTEM.CNF the BIOS reads to find the executable, and --file places the executable on the disc; there is nothing else to put there yet. The result is hello.bin and hello.cue, which any emulator opens. Running it psxemu boots the disc headless and, when stopped, saves what the screen shows:go tool psxemu --bios openbios.bin --disc hello.cue --png hello.png Stop it after a few seconds and hello.png holds the frame: a teal screen with the text in the corner. mednafen and other emulators open the cue sheet directly, and a console that plays burned discs boots it from a CD-R. The next page draws something: a cube from the disc.

The blow demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "blow" (S. Ashley, 1997): a model viewer that blows its model up. A space shuttle, in five pieces, is read off the disc, and one piece at a time is shown at 512 by 240, turned, moved and scaled, under three directional lights, ambient light and fog, every parameter of which a menu of the library's font lets you change. The last page of the menu is the explosion: the piece's polygons fly apart along their normals, flashing white and burning through yellow and red to black while the screen flashes, and then it is put back together to go again. To do that the model is copied at startup with a separate set of vertices for every polygon, since a TMD shares its vertices between the polygons that meet at them, and the copy is what is drawn. R1 and R2 step through the menu's pages and Select and Start through the pieces. On each page the d-pad, L1 and L2 adjust three values, and the symbol buttons the rest: the first page turns the piece, and Triangle and Cross bring the viewpoint nearer and further; the second moves the viewpoint; the third scales the piece; the next three aim and color the lights, Square and Circle choosing the component and Triangle and Cross changing it; then the ambient light; then the fog, its distance and color, and whether it is on; and last the explosion, its speed and whether it is going. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The viewpoint moves in and out by fiftieths, where the original multiplies and divides by 1.02 in floating point. - The model is read off the disc to the address the original's batch script sent it to, and the copy is checked to fit below it. - The model's extent, which the original works out at startup and prints to the serial console, is left out, and so is the missing data's report, which the original would hang on. Nothing allocates after startup.

The breakout demo, in Go. A port of L. Evans's Net Yaroze demo "breakout" (Sony, 1996): Breakout in sprites. A bat slides along the bottom of the screen under a wall of bricks, five rows deep and staggered by half a brick, and a ball bounces between them, off the walls and the ceiling, and off the bat, which nudges it sideways by three quarters of the bat's own speed. Each brick goes with one hit and scores fifty; clearing them all starts the next of ten levels, all alike, and letting the ball past the bat costs one of five lives. When they are gone, or the tenth level is cleared, the score and the high score table are shown. The bat and the bricks are textures off the disc; the ball is the SDK's ball pattern from balltex.h, in one of its thirty-two shades, loaded straight from a table in the program, as the check sample's are. Behind everything a semi-transparent black box softens the sprites' black edges, the library's font prints the frame, the lives and the score, and music plays from a sequence off the disc. Left and right move the bat, and R1 and R2 make it faster and slower. L1 pauses for as long as it is held, and Start and Select together quit. On the score screen Cross starts a new game and L1 and R1 together quit. Differences from the original: - The textures are loaded below the program rather than above it, where the original's batch script put them and where a Go program's data now lies. The sound, as in the check sample, comes from the same files at the same addresses. - The missing data is reported, where the original would hang. Nothing allocates after startup.

The car demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "car" (Sony, 1995, "60frame" in its source): an Alfa Romeo Giulietta, a textured model wearing seven textures, drives in from the distance and then turns slowly at the center of the screen under one light, at 640 by 240 interlaced. The demo is about frame rate: Start switches it between sixty frames a second and thirty, which the library's font reports, and the controls double their steps at thirty so that the car moves at the same speed either way. The d-pad moves the car across and up and down, the symbol buttons turn it, and L1 and L2 bring it nearer and push it further. Select quits. Differences from the original: - The textures and model are read off the disc to addresses below the program. The original's batch script sent them to addresses the Go program occupies. - The drive in moves the car by whole units each frame, as the original's integer coordinate ends up doing: it adds 1 + i/20 in floating point and C truncates the sum towards zero, which rounds the step up while the car is behind the viewpoint. The port reproduces that arithmetic. - The speed line is printed in a font window the port opens. The original prints without opening one. Nothing allocates after startup.

The check sample, in Go. A port of sdk/sample/check/main.c: bouncing balls over a cleared background, the count adjustable with the d-pad, with the sound data read off the disc. It exists to show the Go bindings carrying a real program rather than a hello world, and to put the CD path, the controller and a few hundred sprites through the same code the C sample uses. Two deliberate differences from the original: - The CD waits are bounded. The C sample spins in "while ((cnt = CdReadSync(1, 0)) > 0)" with no limit, so running it without the files present hangs before it has drawn anything. - Sound is only started if the VAB actually loaded. The C sample calls SsSeqSetVol and SsSeqPlay with whatever handle it has, including the zero left behind when the transfer failed. Nothing allocates after startup. With no collector running, anything allocated in the frame loop would never be reclaimed.

The chrome sample, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "chrome" (S. Ashley, 1997): a textured torus, turning, whose texture coordinates are worked out again every frame from its normals as the torus turns, so the texture reads as a reflection of the world rather than paint on the surface. That is chrome, or environment, mapping. It puts the GTE, the 3D library and lighting through their paces, which the check example does not touch. Differences from the original: - The texture and model are read off the disc. On a Net Yaroze the loader's batch script sent them from the PC to fixed addresses; they are loaded to the same addresses. - The torus has a coordinate system of its own. The original points the object at WORLD, the library's nil coordinate system, and then writes its transformation through that pointer every frame, which in C silently overwrites the kernel's memory at address 0. - A loading message, and a report if the data is missing, rather than a black screen. Hold Start and Select together to quit.

The clone sample, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "clone" (S. Ashley, 1997): a first-person maze shooter. Walk a fogged, textured maze, shoot the monsters before they shoot you, pick up first aid, find the pulsing exit, and do it again on the next of three levels. A heart beats louder as monsters get closer. It puts much of the machine to work at once: the GTE and the 3D library, with fog and subdivision, models built in memory, sprites, lines, filled boxes and text, a palette rewritten every frame, and sound effects played straight on SPU voices, which the check example's sequenced music does not use. Controls: the d-pad walks and turns, L1 and R1 sidestep, X fires, and circle shows the map of where you have been. Hold Start and Select together to quit. Differences from the original: - The sound bank, maps and textures are read off the disc. On a Net Yaroze the loader's batch script sent them from the PC to fixed addresses; they are loaded to the same addresses. - Every object has a real coordinate system. The original points them all at WORLD, the library's nil coordinate system, and writes each object's transformation through that pointer, which in C silently overwrites the kernel's memory at address 0. They share one here, as they shared that address there. - Reading the map outside its bounds reads as no walls. The original reads whatever memory is next to the map, which Go does not allow. - The heartbeat's volume starts from zero. The original compares against a variable it never sets. - It shows a loading message, and a report if the data is missing, where the original would hang or exit. Nothing allocates after startup.

The dino demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "dino" (1996): a dinosaur walking in front of a castle, at 640 by 240. The dinosaur is one model of 2,724 polygons, animated by the GTE's vertex interpolation, MIME: the model file comes with a file of vertex differences, nine sets of them, each moving part of the body, a leg, the neck, the eyelids, and every frame the model's vertices are put back as they were and each set is added in some proportion. The proportions come from the controls through a bank of transfer functions, sixteen filters that each smooth their input over the last few frames with a window of weights, so that a button pressed becomes a step taken. The walk itself is four of them cycling through a table. The castle is a full-screen 16-bit picture copied into the drawing buffer every frame before the model is drawn over it, in fog, under three lights. Music plays from a sequence, with reverb. The dinosaur walks by itself. Square and Circle turn it, Triangle and Cross tip it, the d-pad moves it across and up and down, and Start and Select bring it nearer and further. R2 opens its mouth, L2 blinks, R1 turns its head and L1 lifts its tail. Holding L1 and R1 with Select stops the walk and puts the legs on the buttons instead: R1, R2, L1 and L2 lift each in turn, with Down the feet and with Up the knees. L1 and R1 with Start starts the walk again, and then Up and Down choose between the buttons above and R1 and R2 changing the walk's speed, with L1 putting it back. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The data is read off the disc rather than sent over the serial cable, and where it lands is rearranged: the sound comes first, to the addresses the check sample loads it at, and once the sound bank has gone to the SPU the model and its textures are loaded over it. The castle picture is loaded into the program's own memory, since with everything else there is no room for it below the program. - The GPU packet space is the program's own, and larger. The original puts it where the sound bank was, with its two buffers closer together than a frame of the model can need. - The walk's speed, when it is turned down past zero, wraps round the step tables rather than reading before them. Nothing allocates after startup.

A Dog Tale, in Go. A port of Ira Rainey's Net Yaroze game "A Dog Tale" (1997), which went out on the cover disc of the Official UK PlayStation Magazine and on Sony's own Net Yaroze demo discs: a platform game in sprites, twelve screens wide, in which a man sets out across a desert to free his dog, chained up at the far end with five padlocks, by finding the five keys. There are platforms to climb, some of them moving, bones to collect, fifty of which are worth a life, and cacti, which cost one. The desert scrolls in parallax, the two ranges of mountains and the floor each at their own speed under a fixed sky, which is what the author says the game grew out of. The title screen scrolls a message along its foot under a logo that spins in, with an about box that scales in over it, and when the last life goes the screen is grabbed into video memory and spun away to nothing. The tune is Sony's sample, the one the check sample plays, which the author's message says was borrowed. The author's readme asks anyone using the code for a thank you: thanks, Ira. Left and right walk, Cross jumps, straight up or the way you are walking, and Triangle shows the keys found so far. Select pauses, and any direction or Cross goes on; Start while paused gives up and goes back to the title. On the title, left and right choose between About and Play and Cross chooses; Select closes the about box. There is no way to quit the program, as in the original. Differences from the original: - The pictures are read off the disc as the one file the original was sent over the serial cable as, at a lower address, since where the original put them is where a Go program's code now lies. The tune comes from the SDK's own files, as the check sample's does, and the sound bank's body is read into the program's own memory, since with the pictures there is no room for it below the program. The file's first picture, a Net Yaroze logo that a function the source declares but never defines would have shown, is loaded and never used. - Every object has an image description of its own. The original gives each a pointer to one that is never set, and so writes every image's description to address 0. - Objects are checked to be in use before their sizes are read, and the search for the platform under the man stops at the last object. The original reads the sizes of unused objects through null pointers, and one past the end of its array. - There are five keys. The original puts six into the world, reading past the end of its table of five for the last, which lands at the start of the level at whatever height the memory after the table gives. - The pad check reports nothing pressed when neither Select nor Start is, and the title's spin starts from zero. The original leaves both to whatever happened to be in a register or on the stack. Nothing allocates after startup.

The dungeon demo, in Go. A port of "dungeon" (Mizuki, 1996), a demo posted to the Japanese Net Yaroze members' forum, in the form the LPGE team's copy of it took, with a ship added: a maze of stone walls, laid out at random in blocks of three cells, walked through in the first person. Only the cells around the viewpoint are given walls, a ceiling and a floor each frame, as objects in their own coordinate systems, and the nearest are subdivided. A line and two boxes in the corner show which way the viewpoint faces, and the library's font prints where it is. Walls stop the viewpoint, blue fog closes in behind them, and two lights follow the view, one from above and one from below. The directional buttons turn and walk, L1 and R1 sidestep, L2 and R2 look up and down, and Circle makes everything faster. Start switches to steering the ship, which sits near the start: the directional buttons and L1 and L2 move it along its own axes, the symbol buttons and R1 and R2 spin it about them, and Select makes those faster. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The data is read off the disc to the addresses the original's batch script sent it to. The cube model the script also sends, which the program never uses, is left out. - The objects a frame draws are bounded by their array's size, 256. The original goes on filling past its end when more of the maze is in view than that, over the coordinate systems next to it. - The checks for the edge of the maze come before the reads they guard, which the original makes a cell past the edge first. - Quitting returns to the BIOS. The original calls exit.

The flame demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "flame" (S. Ashley, 1997): a sheet of fire, drawn at 640 by 480. A grid of heat values is seeded along its bottom edge with random hot spots every frame, blurred with its neighbors, and scrolled upwards, so that the heat rises, spreads and dies out. The grid is a single TMD built in memory at startup, a flat sheet of gouraud quads with lighting switched off, and every frame the four corner colors of each quad are rewritten from the heat values through a palette running from black through red and yellow to white. The GTE and the 3D library then draw it like any other model, so the sheet can be turned and moved: the d-pad tilts it, L1 and L2 roll it, and R1 and R2 move it nearer and further. The library's font prints the count of horizontal syncs a frame takes. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The heat grid is one row and one column larger than the original's, which reads one past its edges in the blur and so takes whatever is next to the array in memory for the heat beyond them. Here that heat is zero. - The sheet has a coordinate system of its own. The original points it at WORLD, the library's nil coordinate system, and writes its transformation through that pointer, which in C silently overwrites the kernel's memory at address 0. Nothing allocates after startup.

The invaders demo, in Go. A port of L. Evans's Net Yaroze demo "invaders" (Sony, 1996): Space Invaders in sprites. Four rows of eight invaders march across the screen, dropping a line each time they reach a side, and one of them fires back now and then; the player's ship slides along the bottom and shoots upwards, no more than once every ten frames. Clearing the screen starts the next of ten levels, all alike, and an invader or a shot reaching the ship costs one of five lives. When they are gone, or the tenth level is cleared, the score and the high score table are shown. Behind the sprites a semi-transparent black box covers the screen, which the original uses to soften the black edges its sprites have, and the library's font prints the frame, the lives and the score. Music plays from a sequence off the disc. Left and right push the ship, which has momentum, and Triangle fires. L1 pauses for as long as it is held, and Start and Select together quit. On the score screen Cross starts a new game and L1 and R1 together quit. If the invaders reach the bottom of the screen the program ends. Differences from the original: - Positions and speeds are fixed point, with four bits of fraction, where the original has doubles. The only fraction in the game is the player's shot, which moves two and a half pixels a frame. - The textures are loaded below the program rather than above it, where the original's batch script put them and where a Go program's data now lies. The sound, as in the check sample, comes from the same files at the same addresses. - An invader only fires when there is one to fire. The original picks one at random by dividing by how many are left, which is zero in the frame after the last is destroyed, and then indexes its arrays with what that gives. - A shot that cannot be created, with all of them in flight, is not fired. The original writes the shot into the element before the first. - The missing data is reported, where the original would hang. Nothing allocates after startup.

The mdec example: full-color video through the motion decoder. The GPU draws in 15-bit color, but it can show 24-bit pictures, and the MDEC, the PlayStation's motion decoder, is how games made them: it takes pictures compressed much as JPEG compresses them, a 16x16 macroblock at a time, and turns them into pixels, which a program copies into VRAM. Games played their video this way. The Net Yaroze library has no MDEC functions, so this drives the MDEC and its two DMA channels through their registers. The movie, a ray-traced loop that gen renders and format/mdec encodes, is read off the disc whole and played at 20 frames a second. Each frame is decoded a column of macroblocks at a time, while the other is on screen. Hold Start and Select together to quit.

The morph demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "morph" (S. Ashley, 1997): a textured sheet that turns into a cylinder, a torus, a sphere and back into a sheet, at 640 by 480. The sheet is a TMD built in memory at startup, a grid of textured quads over a 256 by 256 picture with lighting off and both faces drawn, and every frame each of its vertices moves one unit towards the matching vertex of the shape it is becoming, so that the shape changes over a few hundred frames while the whole thing tumbles. The library's font prints the count of horizontal syncs a frame takes. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The sheet has a coordinate system of its own. The original points it at WORLD, the library's nil coordinate system, and writes its transformation through that pointer, which in C silently overwrites the kernel's memory at address 0. - The quads' headers carry the lengths the TMD format gives a textured quad without lighting, seven words in and nine out. The original writes six and seven. - The flat sheet's vertices are computed at startup. The other three shapes are the tables the original's mesh generator wrote. Nothing allocates after startup.

The oden demo, in Go. A port of Sony's Net Yaroze demo "oden" (Sony, 1993 to 1996): a demonstration of the lighting calculation. A ball, a cone and a cube, each scaled by its own matrix, stand under three directional lights at 640 by 480 interlaced, and every light can be aimed and recolored while the scene turns. The symbol buttons turn the scene, Start brings it nearer and Select pushes it away. Holding L1, L2 or R2 gives the symbol buttons and the d-pad to the first, second or third light: Triangle and Cross change its red, Circle and Square its green, Select and Start its blue, and the d-pad aims it. Holding R1 with Triangle and Cross raises and lowers the ambient light. The d-pad alone swaps each model for the textured version the TMD also carries, Left the ball, Right the cube and Up the cone, and Down puts the plain versions back. Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The model and texture are read off the disc to addresses below the program. The original's batch script sent them to addresses the Go program occupies. Nothing allocates after startup.

The offscr tutorial, in Go. A port of L. Evans's Net Yaroze tutorial on retexturing at run time (Sony, 1997). A sphere, textured from a 16-bit image, sits over a square of floor. Every frame, after drawing the scene, the program points the drawing environment at the part of VRAM outside the two display buffers where the sphere's texture lives, draws a sprite there, and points it back: the sprite is painted onto the texture, and the sphere wears it from the next frame on. Four seconds in, it also copies a block of VRAM over another, the simplest way to change a texture. The sprite is also drawn on screen, in the top left, as it is. The right-hand buttons move the sprite over the texture, the directional buttons and L1 and L2 move the sphere, Select makes either faster, Start pauses, and Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The data is read off the disc to the addresses the original's batch script sent it to. - What the original prints to the serial console, a line every frame and the drawing environment at the start, is left out. What it shows on screen is kept. - The second ordering tables, through which the sprite is drawn onto the texture, have the two entries their length of 1 gives them. The original declares them an entry long, so clearing one writes past its end into whatever follows; here that was the view. - Code the original never runs is left out: the sprite placement for objects drawn as sprites, of which it has none, and the palette copy it has commented out.

The tunnel tutorial, in Go. A port of L. Evans's Net Yaroze game demo "tunnel" (Sony, 1997), the last of the tutorial series it was built up over: a ship flying down an endless tunnel, shooting waves of enemies. The tunnel is rings of four scaled squares that slide towards the ship and go round to the far end again; the near ones are subdivided so the perspective holds up. Fog, three colored lights, one of them always circling, and semi-transparent sprites for shots, explosions and pick-ups make it the most of the machine's lighting any of the examples use. Its sound is a VAB: a tune started once and left playing, and sound effects keyed on and off by hand. The score is drawn in sprites cut from a font texture. Enemies come in waves: helixes of fighters circling as they come, some switching direction or darting as one, lone attackers that jiggle, evade or circle while they fire, swarms of insect ships, and every so often a robot. Pick-ups give a life, faster shots or movement, or set the lights or the view swinging. The game gets faster every thousand frames. The directional buttons and L1 and L2 move the ship, R1 fires, Select makes moves faster, Select and L2 step slowly, Start pauses, and Start and Select together quit. Differences from the original: - The data is read off the disc to the addresses the original's batch script sent it to. - The random numbers are seeded with a constant. The original seeds them from the seconds of the time it was compiled. - Quitting returns to the BIOS. The original first saves the screen to RAM for the serial console to fetch, and calls exit. - The direction a shot is fired in is normalised in integers, exactly; the original uses floating point. - What the original prints to the serial console is left out, and so are its assertions.
